summary: The Aion V is the first electric SUV from GAC, which launched in Australia in December 2025, and it undercuts most mid-size rivals while quoting a longer 510km WLTP range than the Geely EX5 and matching the dearer BYD Atto 3 Evo Premium. Reviewers rate the cabin quality, quietness and standard equipment highly and find the ride comfortable if unexciting, but consistently criticise the touchscreen-only controls and the intrusive driver-monitoring and speed-sign systems. Both grades share one 150kW front-drive powertrain and a 75.26kWh (usable) LFP battery, so the choice between them is purely about trim rather than range or performance.
pros: 510km WLTP range from a 75.26kWh usable LFP pack, ahead of the Geely EX5 (475km) and level with the BYD Atto 3 Evo Premium for $4,400 less
180kW peak DC charging with a claimed 24-minute 20-80 per cent, roughly double the Geely EX5's peak rate

8-year/unlimited-km vehicle warranty and 8-year/200,000km battery warranty for private buyers, with no dealer-servicing condition, longer than BYD's 6 years or Geely's 7 (commercial use drops to 5 years/150,000km)
Heat pump, V2L, panoramic sunroof, surround-view camera and heated/ventilated front seats are standard on the $42,590 base Premium
5-star ANCAP rating (2025 datestamp, valid to December 2031) applying to both grades
cons: No towing rating at all (GAC publishes none and EV Database lists no tow hitch), against 1500kg braked for a Leapmotor C10 or BYD Atto 3 Evo Premium
Everything runs through the 14.6-inch touchscreen, with no volume dial and mirror adjustment buried in menus
Driver-monitoring and speed-limit warnings are intrusive and reset to on at every start, a recurring complaint across Australian reviews
Highway consumption climbs past 25kWh/100km against the 16.7kWh/100km WLTP claim, so the 510km figure is urban-biased
Brand-new to Australia with about 19 dealers as at March 2026 and no published capped-price service prices as of CarExpert's September 2026 review, leaving resale and running costs unproven
